items.prompt: In a pitch, who does most of the talking?
choices: The buyer
The seller
Both equally
A third party
items.explanation: A pitch is the seller telling the prospect what they do and what it costs.

items.prompt: What is the seller's main job in discovery?
choices: Show features
Quote a price
Handle objections
Ask and listen
items.explanation: Discovery reverses the structure: the prospect talks and the seller listens closely.

items.prompt: Priya's original ask was pricing for how many people?
choices: Eight people
Three people
Six people
Twenty-four people
items.explanation: She asked about an 8-seat plan before any questions were asked.

items.prompt: Why did Doctor B ask questions before prescribing?
choices: The patient had been dishonest about it
Rules require a quiz
The request was a first guess
B had no time to write
items.explanation: The patient's request was their best guess at the cause, not a diagnosis.

items.prompt: Bex's deal was how many times the original ask?
choices: Two times
Three times
Six times
Twelve times
items.explanation: $28,800 divided by $4,800 is 6.

items.prompt: Why had Priya not mentioned the three-team problem at first?
choices: Nobody had asked questions that surfaced it
She wanted to hide it from sellers
The vendor had fixed the handoffs
She did not know the price yet
items.explanation: She was not lying; the bigger problem simply had not been drawn out.

items.prompt: Can an accurate pitch still lose the deal?
choices: No, accuracy is all that matters
No, only price decides which deals close
Yes, but only if the rep is rude
Yes, if it answers the wrong problem
items.explanation: A confident, accurate answer to a problem that is not the real one still loses.

items.prompt: In discovery, what sets the ceiling on the deal?
choices: The rep's talk time
The real problem's scope and cost
The number of seats the buyer first requested
The length of the demo
items.explanation: The first request caps a pitch-first deal; the real problem caps a discovery-first one.

items.prompt: A prospect asks for a quote for 8 seats. The rep gives an accurate demo and the prospect goes quiet. Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: The demo showed several features the product does not actually have
The ask was a first guess and the demo answered it unchecked
The quoted price was higher than any comparable 8-seat tool on offer
The prospect disliked the way the rep spoke during the demo
items.explanation: The pattern matches Adri's call: nothing in the call tested whether the stated ask was the real problem, so the polite silence says the pitch did not connect to anything the prospect cares about.
items.reference:
Pitch versus discovery
📣 Pitch: the seller talks, answers the stated ask
❓ Discovery: the seller asks, the prospect talks
💰 Deal size follows the real problem, not the first request
Why: an accurate pitch to the wrong problem still loses.
items.learnMore:
The stated ask is a first guess

Like the patient who asks for antibiotics, a prospect describes the problem as they currently see it. Discovery checks that view before anything is pitched.

Common mistake

Treating the stated ask as the whole problem and answering it immediately.
items.reflection: Think of a time someone answered exactly what you asked and it still did not help. What question could they have asked first?

items.prompt: Which of these calls actually contains discovery?
choices: The rep presents the pricing tiers, then asks which one fits best
The rep reads out a feature list and then invites any questions
The rep asks what prompted the search, then listens for minutes
The rep emails a recorded demo and waits for the prospect to reply
items.explanation: Discovery is defined by who is talking and what is being learned. The others are all the seller presenting, even when they end in a question.

items.prompt: A rep asks good questions for forty minutes and finds the stated ask was exactly right. What was the discovery worth?
choices: It confirmed the ask, so the pitch can proceed with confidence
Nothing, because the ask was already correct before the call began
It proves discovery only helps when the stated ask turns out wrong
It shows the prospect should have been screened out much earlier
items.explanation: Discovery does not guarantee a bigger deal. Its value is that the pitch now rests on a checked fact instead of an unchecked guess.

items.prompt: Which of these is an open question?
choices: Is 8 seats right?
Do you need reporting?
Is the budget approved?
What is driving this search?
items.explanation: It has no fixed answer shape and carries no guess.

items.prompt: What answer shape does a closed question usually get?
choices: A rambling personal story
Yes, no or a number
A detailed process diagram
A list of every grievance
items.explanation: Closed questions have a small fixed set of possible answers.

items.prompt: Where does the seller's guess hide in a closed question?
choices: In the prospect's reply
In the rep's job title
In the price list
In the wording itself
items.explanation: 'Do you need better reporting?' already assumes reporting is the gap.

items.prompt: When are closed questions best used?
choices: To confirm a detail late in the call
As the opening line of every single call
To avoid hearing the prospect talk
Never, they are banned
items.explanation: Once the problem is understood, closed questions pin down details efficiently.

items.prompt: Which turns 'Is the handoff slow?' into an open question?
choices: Is it slow or fast?
Would a faster handoff help the team much?
What tends to go wrong in the handoff?
Handoffs are slow, right?
items.explanation: It asks the prospect to name the friction in their own words.

items.prompt: Doctor B asked 'When does the cough get worse?' Open or closed?
choices: Closed, because it names a symptom
Closed, because it is about one cough
Open, the patient describes it freely
Open, because it ends with a question mark
items.explanation: The patient fills in the answer; nothing is suggested.

items.prompt: Why do open questions surface unstated problems?
choices: The prospect supplies the framing
They sound friendlier than closed ones
They force a yes from the prospect
They skip the situation step
items.explanation: The problem tends to appear in the prospect's own vocabulary, which the seller could not have guessed.

items.prompt: 'The main issue is speed, right?' is what kind of question?
choices: Open, because it is polite
Open, because it mentions speed
Closed, because it is short
Closed, with the guess built in
items.explanation: It states the seller's assumption and asks for agreement.

items.prompt: A rep says 'So the pain point is response time, right?' and the prospect says 'Yeah, I guess.' What is the best reading?
choices: Evidence that response time is the real problem
A soft agreement with the rep's framing, not evidence
Proof that the prospect has no other problem worth raising
A buying signal strong enough to move on to pricing
items.explanation: A leading closed question tends to get soft, uncommitted agreement even when it is not quite right. The prospect did not generate that answer from their own situation.
items.reference:
Closed versus open
🔒 Closed: yes, no or a number; the guess is in the wording
🔓 Open: a story in the prospect's own words
⏱️ Open early to find the problem, closed late to confirm details
Why: an open question lets the prospect supply the framing instead of accepting yours.
items.learnMore:
Where the assumption lives

A closed question carries the seller's guess inside it, so a yes teaches little. An open question carries no guess, so the answer is new information.

Common mistake

Phrasing a leading question as if it were open, then hearing a soft yes as evidence.
items.reflection: Recall a conversation where a leading question got you to agree with something you only half believed. How would you have wanted it asked?

items.prompt: Which is the best open rewrite of 'Do you want faster reporting?'
choices: Would faster reporting be useful to your whole team this year?
What takes the longest when you pull numbers together today?
Is reporting speed your single biggest concern right now?
Do you want reporting delivered daily or weekly?
items.explanation: Only the first hands the floor over without presupposing that reporting speed is the gap. The others all still contain it.

items.prompt: Late in a call, once the problem is clear, a rep asks 'So that is 24 seats across three teams?' Is that a mistake?
choices: Yes, closed questions never belong in a discovery call
Yes, it should have come before the problem step
No, closed fits when confirming a surfaced detail
No, but only because the prospect answered fast
items.explanation: Closed questions are the right tool for confirming specifics. The error is using them first, before the real problem is understood.

items.prompt: What is the correct order of the four steps?
choices: Situation, problem, implication, need-payoff
Problem, situation, need-payoff, implication
Implication, situation, problem, need-payoff
Need-payoff, problem, situation, implication
items.explanation: Each step sets up the next: setup, friction, cost, value.

items.prompt: Which step asks about the current setup?
choices: Problem
Implication
Need-payoff
Situation
items.explanation: Situation questions establish how things work today.

items.prompt: Which step asks what the friction costs?
choices: Situation
Implication
Problem
Need-payoff
items.explanation: Implication attaches a cost to the friction.

items.prompt: Which step asks what solving it would be worth?
choices: Situation
Problem
Implication
Need-payoff
items.explanation: Need-payoff asks the prospect to state the value of fixing it.

items.prompt: Which step names the specific friction?
choices: Problem
Situation
Implication
Need-payoff
items.explanation: The problem step asks what goes wrong in the setup.

items.prompt: Bex asked how work moves through Priya's team. Which step?
choices: Problem
Implication
Situation
Need-payoff
items.explanation: It maps the setup before any friction is named.

items.prompt: Why keep the situation step short?
choices: Prospects generally dislike talking about themselves for long
It has no value to the seller
It only exists to make the problem question sharp
The flow allows one question per call
items.explanation: It can feel like small talk, so it is easy to over-invest in.

items.prompt: Does each step try to do the next step's job?
choices: No, each builds on the one before
Yes, to save time
Yes, steps are interchangeable
No, because short calls skip every step
items.explanation: Each question is sharp because the previous answer set it up.

items.prompt: A rep opens with 'What tends to go wrong in your handoffs?' without any setup. What is the likely cost?
choices: The prospect will refuse to answer any open question after that
The rep breaks the rule that the problem step comes last
None, since the situation step is optional on every call
The rep cannot judge how big or typical the answer is
items.explanation: Situation gives the context that makes a problem answer interpretable. Without it, 'stuff gets missed' could mean two teams or twenty.
items.reference:
The four steps in order
🧭 Situation: what is the setup today?
⚠️ Problem: what is the friction in it?
💸 Implication: what does the friction cost?
🎯 Need-payoff: what would solving it be worth?
Why: each step builds on the last and does not do the next step's job.
items.learnMore:
A shape, not a script

The order keeps the call focused without turning it into an interrogation. Each question is asked because the previous answer made it sharp.

Common mistake

Spending the whole call on situation questions, or jumping from problem straight to the pitch.
items.reflection: Pick a decision you helped someone make. Which of the four steps did the conversation cover, and which did it skip?

items.prompt: 'When a handoff gets missed, does it show up in cost?' belongs to which step?
choices: Problem, because it mentions a handoff that gets missed
Implication, because it asks what the friction costs
Situation, because it describes how work flows
Need-payoff, because it ends on cost
items.explanation: The friction is already named; the question moves on to its consequences, which is the implication step.

items.prompt: A prospect volunteers a cost in minute one ('we lose $6,000 each time'). What should the rep do?
choices: Restart at situation to respect the order
Use it, then fill in the situation and problem behind it
Skip every remaining step and quote a price
Ask the need-payoff question and drop the rest
items.explanation: The order is a guide to coverage, not a rule against hearing things early. A stated cost still needs the setup and friction that explain it.

items.prompt: What does implication add to the problem step?
choices: A longer feature list
A quote the buyer can sign
A cost attached to the friction
A summary of the setup
items.explanation: A problem names the friction; implication says what it costs.

items.prompt: Priya's last rush fee was about how much?
items.explanation: She said the last one was about $6,000.

items.prompt: How many rush fees did Priya's team pay this quarter?
choices: One
Five
Seven
Three
items.explanation: She mentioned three times this quarter.

items.prompt: If all three fees were similar to $6,000, the quarter's total is about?
items.explanation: 3 x 6,000 = 18,000. This is an assumption made for the example.

items.prompt: The plan costs $28,800 a year. What is that per quarter?
Without an implication figure, what lacks an anchor?
choices: The price quoted later
The opening greeting
The company name
The seat count
items.explanation: Neither side has a comparison point for judging the price.

items.prompt: Which of these is an implication answer?
choices: Handoffs sometimes slip between the teams involved
We use Slack and a shared doc
We paid three rush fees this quarter
Three teams touch each request
items.explanation: It states a cost. The others are problem or situation answers.

items.prompt: What happens to urgency if implication is skipped?
choices: It rises because the pitch is longer
It becomes the buyer's job alone
It stays as mild as the problem sounded
It disappears and the call ends
items.explanation: The seller then has to manufacture urgency, which is harder.

items.prompt: Why does a $7,200-a-quarter plan look small next to about $18,000 of assumed rush fees?
choices: The surfaced cost gives the price a comparison point
Discounts apply once a prospect has named a cost
Quarterly prices are always lower than the annual price shown
Rush fees are refunded to buyers by law
items.explanation: Without the cost on the table the price has nothing to be compared against. With it, the price reads as smaller than the problem it fixes.
items.reference:
What implication adds
⚠️ Problem answer: handoffs sometimes slip
💸 Implication answer: 3 rush fees this quarter, last about $6,000
⚖️ Price now has something to be compared against
Why: a cost turns a mild problem into a felt one and anchors the price.
items.learnMore:
Cost makes the problem felt

A problem without a cost leaves urgency mild. A cost the prospect stated themselves gives both sides a comparison point for the price.

Common mistake

Accepting a vague cost and moving on, or inventing the figure for the prospect.
items.reflection: Think of a nagging problem in your own life. What would it take to put an honest cost on it, and would that change what you did?

items.prompt: A prospect's cost answer is a guess: 'maybe a few thousand.' How should the rep treat it?
choices: As a firm number to put in the proposal
As worthless, so the cost question is dropped
As proof the prospect will not buy at any price
As a start to probe with a concrete event
items.explanation: A guess is a signal that the cost has not been examined yet. Asking about a specific past event usually produces something sturdier.

💸 Implication answer: 3 rush fees this quarter, last about $6,000

Stuff gets missed / rush fees and a missed launch
Three rush fees / we use a shared doc
A missed launch / pricing for eight people
items.explanation: The problem answer names the friction, and the implication answer is the consequence of that same friction. The other pairs mix steps or unrelated facts.

items.prompt: In need-payoff, who states why solving it matters?
choices: The seller
The prospect
The seller's manager
A neutral analyst
items.explanation: The point is that the prospect says it in their own words.

items.prompt: Which sounds like a need-payoff answer?
choices: This tool is going to save you a very large amount of money
Our plan includes twenty-four seats
One fewer missed launch is worth more than this tool
Handoffs happen in Slack and a doc
items.explanation: It states the value of fixing the problem, spoken by the prospect.

items.prompt: Why is a seller-asserted payoff weaker?
choices: The prospect weighs it as a sales claim
Sellers are not allowed to mention value at all in a call
It is always factually wrong
It makes the call longer
items.explanation: Claims from the seller get discounted by default.

items.prompt: Why does Bex ask 'what would it be worth to you?'
choices: So Bex can avoid quoting a price
So Bex can end the call early
So the prospect feels rushed
So the prospect states the value themselves
items.explanation: The prospect's own words carry further than the seller's.

items.prompt: Which later unit turns the payoff figure into a formal case?
choices: requirements-gathering
value-based-selling
validation
bounded-contexts
items.explanation: Discovery surfaces the number; value-based selling formalizes it.

items.prompt: What did Priya say leadership would do with a bigger plan?
choices: Cancel the budget
Refuse all new tools
Ask for a cheaper plan
Sign off on it
items.explanation: She said leadership would actually sign off if the other two teams were on it too.

items.prompt: Whose words carry further inside the prospect's company?
choices: The prospect's own words
The seller's brochure
The seller's closing email
The feature list
items.explanation: People repeat their own reasons in internal discussions.

items.prompt: Is need-payoff a polished ROI case?
choices: Yes, it is a finished ROI model
Yes, it replaces the price quote
No, it is the raw value the prospect states
No, it is the seller's discount offer
items.explanation: Discovery surfaces the number; it does not polish it.

items.prompt: A seller says 'You will save a fortune' and the prospect shrugs. What is the structural problem?
choices: The seller's payoff was far too specific for the prospect
The seller skipped the situation step before the pitch
The seller asserted the payoff instead of the prospect
The prospect had not yet seen a demo of the product
items.explanation: A payoff in the seller's mouth is a claim to be weighed. The same idea spoken by the prospect, after walking through the cost, becomes their own reason.
items.reference:
Who says it matters
🗣️ Seller says: this will save you a lot
🙋 Prospect says: one fewer missed launch is worth more than the tool
🧾 The second becomes the raw input for a later ROI case
Why: a reason the prospect states is theirs; one the seller asserts is only an argument.
items.learnMore:
Let the prospect say it

After walking through the cost, the prospect can state what fixing it is worth. That statement is in their words and carries into their own internal discussions.

Common mistake

Declaring the benefit on the prospect's behalf because it feels faster.
items.reflection: When did you last change your mind because you said the reason out loud yourself rather than being told it?

items.prompt: Which question best elicits a need-payoff answer?
choices: If handoffs stopped slipping, what would change for you?
Don't you think fewer slipped handoffs would be quite valuable?
Our plan prevents slips, so shall we go ahead and proceed?
How many handoffs slipped last quarter, and in which month?
items.explanation: It hands the value judgment to the prospect without suggesting the answer. The others lead, close, or return to the problem step.

The cost may not be felt yet, so revisit implication
items.explanation: A lukewarm payoff usually means the cost was never made concrete. Going back to implication is more productive than pushing forward.

items.prompt: A prospect says 'it is fine, we manage.' Best next move?
choices: Repeat the same question word for word
Ask about one concrete event
Skip to the price
End the call politely
items.explanation: A concrete memory is easier to answer than an abstract question.

items.prompt: Why is a concrete memory easier than a dollar estimate?
choices: It keeps the prospect quiet and relaxed throughout
It asks for recall, not instant arithmetic
It always yields a bigger number
It removes the need for the problem step
items.explanation: Describing what happened takes no calculation.

items.prompt: If a prospect never engages with cost even when concrete, what does it signal?
choices: The rep asked in the wrong order
The prospect is hiding a competitor from the rep
The problem may not hurt enough to buy a fix
The seat count is wrong
items.explanation: No rephrasing creates urgency that is not there.

items.prompt: What was Bex's pitch, once it came?
choices: One sentence plus a request to demo
A fifteen-minute feature tour
A full written proposal
A recorded video
items.explanation: Priya had already said why it mattered, so the pitch only had to point at one capability.

items.prompt: On a multi-stakeholder call, what can divergent answers show?
choices: The prospect is unprepared
Only one stakeholder is correct
The call should be ended right away
The real problem may be several related ones
items.explanation: Different people feel the same issue in different ways.

items.prompt: Who cared about the rush fees themselves in the example?
choices: The engineering lead
The finance director
Priya, the ops manager
The client's team
items.explanation: The finance director cared about the fees, not the workflow behind them.

items.prompt: Who cared about being pulled in with no warning?
choices: The finance director
Priya, the ops manager
The client's team
The engineering lead
items.explanation: The engineering lead's concern was interruption, not cost.

items.prompt: Is Priya's call the whole territory?
choices: No, it is one clean case among messier ones
Yes, every call goes the same way
Yes, the flow guarantees clean answers
No, because real calls have no steps
items.explanation: The unit asks the reader to extend it to evasive, reputational and non-decider cases.

items.prompt: The finance director gives a precise cost; the engineering lead gives a vague, uncomfortable one. What should the rep do?
choices: Take the finance number as the whole picture and pitch to it
Move on quickly so the call stays calm and agreeable for everyone
Name the gap gently and ask how it shows up for each person
Ask the engineering lead to accept the finance figure as given
items.explanation: The gap itself is a finding. A pitch built on only one voice risks losing the person whose team has to use the tool.
items.reference:
When the call gets messy
🙈 Evasive prospect: ask about one concrete event
👥 Several voices: let each answer, then ask about the gap
🚫 No cost even when concrete: the problem may not hurt enough
Why: a messy answer is information, not a reason to smooth over or drop the question.
items.learnMore:
The clean call is one case

Priya's call had a clear answer at every step. Real calls have deflection, conflict between stakeholders and costs that are hard to count.

Common mistake

Smoothing over disagreement to keep the call comfortable.
items.reflection: Think of a meeting where two people described the same problem very differently. What did the difference tell you?

items.prompt: A prospect says they have never added up the cost. Which follow-up is most likely to yield a usable answer?
choices: Can you estimate the total annual cost to the nearest dollar?
Most companies lose a lot at this stage, would you agree?
You mentioned a missed launch. What happened with the client?
Is the cost higher than our plan's annual price, yes or no?
items.explanation: It swaps arithmetic for a specific memory. The others demand a figure cold, lead the answer, or compress it into a closed yes or no.

When the call gets messy
🙈 Evasive prospect: ask about one concrete event
👥 Several voices: let each answer, then ask about the gap
🚫 No cost even when concrete: the problem may not hurt enough
Why: a messy answer is information, not a reason to smooth over or drop the question.
items.learnMore:
The clean call is one case

Priya's call had a clear answer at every step. Real calls have deflection, conflict between stakeholders and costs that are hard to count.

Common mistake

Smoothing over disagreement to keep the call comfortable.
items.reflection: Think of a meeting where two people described the same problem very differently. What did the difference tell you?

items.prompt: On a call where the real cost is reputational, what adjusts in the flow?
choices: Implication still applies, but the answer may be a story or risk
Implication is skipped, since only dollar figures count in discovery
Need-payoff is replaced by the seller's own estimate of the value
Situation repeats until the prospect finally names a dollar number
items.explanation: The flow's purpose is to surface what the problem costs. When that cost is hard to count, the question stays and the shape of the answer changes.
